analysis.one_line_summary: Current Letta (letta-code) stores agent memory as Markdown files in a per-agent git repository ("MemFS"; one scope covers agent memory, skills and shared repos). Git commits are the revisions. Prompt compilation is pinned to the HEAD SHA and redone when HEAD changes. Background "reflection"/memory-worker subagents write on isolated git worktree branches and merge back. Shared memory is extra git repos attached to several agents, synced by push / pull --rebase. Writers are serialized with a pid-fenced file lease. Commits are gated by pre-commit validation (read_only, size, layout). The retired V1 server had DB "blocks" with an optimistic-lock version column, linear undo/redo history, and a many-to-many block-agent table that rebuilt every attached agent's prompt on change. Neither version has a dependency/justification graph, transitive invalidation, or certificate-checked actions.
analysis.architecture:
CURRENT (letta-code, TypeScript/Bun, Apache-2.0):
- Storage. Each agent's memory is a git working copy at ~/.letta/agents/{id}/memory (src/agent/memory-git.ts getMemoryRepoDir, cloneMemoryRepo, initializeLocalMemoryRepo).
- Remote mode. The origin is a Letta Cloud git remote (getGitRemoteUrl), with an optional mirror to a user GitHub repo through a post-commit hook (memory-git-hooks.ts POST_COMMIT_HOOK_SCRIPT, pushToMemoryRepository).
- Local mode. The backend (src/backend/local/local-backend.ts, local-store.ts) keeps agent, conversation and compiled-prompt records on disk, and memory is a local-only git repo.
- Data model. A memory item is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter: description, plus a protected read_only field. Layouts are memfs-v1 (system/ and reference/ dirs) and memfs-v2 (a root MEMORY.md plus projected child MEMORY.md indexes). Skills live at skills/<name>/SKILL.md, and .memfs.config.json holds constraints.
- Wiki-links [[...]] between memory files are parsed only for a UI graph view (src/websocket/listener/commands/memory.ts extractMemoryReferences).
- Process model. There is one CLI/App Server process per user. The primary agent edits memory files with ordinary Write/Edit/ApplyPatch tools. Subagents (reflection, "dreaming", memory workers, conflict-repair workers) run in separate processes, kernel-sandboxed and limited to their own memory dir (src/memory-confinement.ts, src/permissions/memory-confinement-launcher.ts).
- Post-turn sync commits, pushes and rebases (memory-git.ts syncPendingMemoryCommitsAfterTurn; attached-repository-git-sync.ts).
- API surface:
  - The `memory` tool (src/tools/impl/memory.ts) is a read-only directory/file viewer. There is no dedicated write tool; writes go through the generic file tools.
  - The App Server websocket protocol (src/types/protocol_v2.ts) has memory_history (git log per file), memory_file_at_ref (read a file at a SHA), memory_commit_diff, read/write memory file, a memory_updated push event (affected_paths), and conversation_recompile.
  - Cloud REST: GET /v1/agents/{id}/repositories (src/agent/attached-repositories.ts) and agents.blocks.list.
  - The MCP code is client-side only (src/mcp-client.ts, backend/api/unified-mcp.ts). Letta does not expose memory as an MCP server.
  - Hooks: PreToolUse (can block or rewrite input), PostToolUse, PermissionRequest, and others (src/hooks/types.ts).

RETIRED V1 (letta archive, Python/FastAPI/SQLAlchemy/Postgres):
- `block` table with a version_id_col optimistic lock (letta/orm/block.py lines 53-61).
- `block_history` with sequence_number undo/redo (letta/orm/block_history.py).
- `blocks_agents` M:N for shared blocks.
- REST /v1/blocks and /v1/agents/{id}/core-memory.

mechanisms.name: Git commits as immutable memory revisions (MemFS)
mechanisms.how_it_works: Every memory change is a git commit on main in the agent's memory repo. commitMemoryWrite stages only the given pathspecs (git add -A -- paths), commits with the agent as author and returns the new SHA. Unstaged paths are untouched. A failed commit unstages them. History is git log. Old versions can be read with memory_file_at_ref (a git SHA) and memory_history (per-file log). Supersession means a new commit on the same path. There is no per-item 'supersedes' pointer and no per-file version number; the commit SHA covers the whole tree.
mechanisms.evidence: letta-code/src/agent/memory-git.ts commitMemoryWrite (~L1234), commitMemoryPaths (~L1184), stageMemoryPaths, getMemoryHeadRevision (L1300, exported but unused); src/types/protocol_v2.ts MemoryHistoryCommand / MemoryFileAtRefCommand (~L1005-1027); src/websocket/listener/commands/memory.ts
mechanisms.limitations: Versions cover the whole repo, not each item. There are no logical heads per item and no CAS on an expected item revision. The primary agent edits the working tree directly, so uncommitted edits are invisible to other processes until the post-turn commit.
mechanisms.why: Validates ContextDB's immutable-revision plus content-address model. A tree-hash snapshot gives cheap, consistent 'Pin' reads. ContextDB should keep per-item heads but could expose a repo-wide snapshot id (as git does) for reproducible context reads, and could offer git export/mirroring as a product feature.

mechanisms.name: Revision-pinned compiled context with recompile on HEAD change
mechanisms.how_it_works: compileLocalSystemPrompt reads memory only from committed HEAD (git ls-tree / git show HEAD:path), never the working tree. It records memfsRevision = HEAD SHA and rawSystemHash. getOrCompileSystemPrompt compares the stored (rawSystemHash, memfsRevision) with the current values. If both match, it reuses the cached prompt. If only the memory revision changed, it compiles a dry run and appends a <memory_update> message mid-conversation. That message names the new revision and says it overrides earlier memory. This keeps the prompt cache intact rather than rewriting the system message. If the system prompt changed, it fully recompiles. After a memory subagent finishes, recompiles are coalesced per conversation (recompileByConversation map).
mechanisms.evidence: letta-code/src/backend/local/system-prompt-compilation.ts getCommittedMemfsRevision (L65), collectCommittedMemoryFiles (L81), compileLocalSystemPrompt (L432); src/backend/local/local-backend.ts formatMidConversationMemoryUpdate (~L170), getOrCompileSystemPrompt (~L918-965); src/cli/helpers/memory-subagent-completion.ts
mechanisms.limitations: Staleness is detected only at the granularity of the whole repo HEAD, and only when the next turn starts. It does not know which parts of the context, or which earlier decisions, depended on the changed files. Nothing is invalidated transitively, and actions already taken are not checked again.
mechanisms.why: This is a working, simple form of a certified context read: the packed context carries the revision it was built from, and the revision is compared before reuse. ContextDB should do the same with a set of per-item (id, rev) pins plus a frontier token. It should also reuse the 'delta message instead of rewriting the prefix' trick to keep LLM prompt caching. That addresses a practical product problem the spec does not cover.

mechanisms.name: Isolated worktree branches for background memory writers, merged back
mechanisms.how_it_works: createReflectionMemoryWorktree runs `git worktree add -b letta/<label>/<id> <baseHead>` from the parent's HEAD. The subagent's filesystem scope is writable only in its worktree and read-only for the parent (buildReflectionMemoryScope). finalizeReflectionMemoryWorktreeUnlocked returns a typed outcome: no_changes, dirty_uncommitted, failed (subagent unsuccessful), parent_dirty, merge_conflict, or merged. Leftover uncommitted changes and a dirty parent both abort with a retryable status. Otherwise it refreshes the parent from origin, then runs `git merge`, and on conflict `git merge --abort` and reports merge_conflict (retryable; transcript re-processed). A requireAlreadyMerged mode checks `merge-base --is-ancestor` when the primary agent itself was asked to integrate. integrateMemoryWorkerWorktree does the same for memory workers, keeping the branch on conflict so nothing is lost.
mechanisms.evidence: letta-code/src/agent/memory-worktree.ts createReflectionMemoryWorktree (L125), buildReflectionMemoryScope (L191), finalizeReflectionMemoryWorktreeUnlocked (L363-657), finalizeReflectionMemoryWorktree (L659, wraps withMemoryOperation), integrateMemoryWorkerWorktree (L685)
mechanisms.limitations: Conflicts are textual at line level in git. There is no semantic conflict notion and no record of what the branch read. A clean textual merge can still combine contradictory facts. Reflection results are discarded and recomputed rather than rebased.
mechanisms.why: This is a proven pattern for speculative writes by background agents: a branch from a base revision, then a merge or abort with typed outcomes. It maps onto ContextDB's base-revision CAS and PENDING semantics. ContextDB can do better by merging per item and running a read-set validation (which items did the worker read and are they still current) instead of a line diff.

mechanisms.name: Checkout lease: pid+start-time fenced O_EXCL file lock
mechanisms.how_it_works: claimMemoryOperation acquires <gitdir>/letta-memory-operation.lock through tryAcquireFileLock. The lock is created with link() from a temp file, so creation is atomic O_EXCL-style. With reapOnlyDeadOwner the lock is reaped only when the holder pid plus process start time is gone. A paused holder keeps the lock, and an AbortSignal is the only way to give up waiting. withMemoryOperation wraps harness writers: worktree finalize, conflict repair, post-turn sync. The primary agent's own edits deliberately do not take the lock. Workers stage only their own files, so a race shows up as a git conflict. Per-path promise chaining in repositorySyncs serializes syncs of the same shared repo inside one process.
mechanisms.evidence: letta-code/src/agent/memory-operation.ts claimMemoryOperation, withMemoryOperation; src/utils/file-lock.ts (L40-220, link(), reapOnlyDeadOwner); src/agent/attached-repository-git-sync.ts syncPendingAttachedRepositoryCommits (repositorySyncs map)
mechanisms.limitations: A coarse lock on the whole checkout, local to one machine. Remote concurrency relies on git non-fast-forward rejection. The primary agent is unlocked by design, so it is not a full transaction system. There is no CAS on an expected version.
mechanisms.why: Fencing with liveness (pid plus start time) and leaving the main interactive writer unlocked are pragmatic choices that hold up in practice. For ContextDB, per-head CAS replaces the coarse lock. The liveness-fenced lease is still useful for the single-writer daemon/WAL owner and for background maintenance jobs.

mechanisms.name: Remote sync: push, then pull --rebase on non-fast-forward, with conflict status
mechanisms.how_it_works: syncPendingMemoryCommitsAfterTurn checks status --porcelain for MERGE_HEAD/rebase dirs and unmerged codes (getMemoryConflictSummary), then dirty, then ahead/behind (getMemoryAheadBehind). It validates pending commits and pushes. On a non-fast-forward error (isNonFastForwardPushError) it runs pull --rebase, checks for conflicts again, validates again, and pushes. It returns a typed status: clean, pushed, dirty, conflict, invalid, push_failed, or skipped. That status becomes a system reminder for the agent. pullMemory tries ff-only, then rebase. With unrelated history it resets to origin/main after saving the old local HEAD as refs/letta-backup/pre-sync-<ts>, and refuses to do so if the tree is dirty.
mechanisms.evidence: letta-code/src/agent/memory-git.ts syncPendingMemoryCommitsAfterTurn (L1837-1985), pullMemory (L1589-1680), recoverMemoryPullByResettingToRemote (L1069-1125), getMemoryConflictSummary (L1768)
mechanisms.limitations: The remote ref acts as a single global CAS register (the branch tip). Rebase silently interleaves two agents' edits when no text conflicts. There is no semantic validation of the rebased state beyond frontmatter and constraints.
mechanisms.why: It shows the 'optimistic push, retry on head moved' loop working at scale with LLM agents, and that a typed sync status surfaced to the agent as a reminder is workable UX. ContextDB's CAS-on-head with typed conflict results is the same loop per item. The backup-ref-before-destructive-reset is worth copying.

mechanisms.name: Token-fenced repair-attempt records (dedupe conflict repair workers)
mechanisms.how_it_works: claimMemoryConflictRepair computes a signature of the conflict state (HEAD plus MERGE_HEAD/REBASE_HEAD/... or the invalid-history description). It stores {signature, token(uuid), state: launching|done, pid, started} in <gitdir>/letta-memory-repair.json under a file lock. If the same signature is already done, it returns attempted, so the agent is told instead of a worker being relaunched every turn. If the holder pid is alive, it returns in_progress. A crashed holder is retried. Later transitions (complete/clear) apply only when the token matches, so a late worker cannot overwrite a newer claim.
mechanisms.evidence: letta-code/src/agent/memory-conflict-repair.ts claimMemoryConflictRepair (L161), completeMemoryConflictRepair (L212), clearMemoryConflictRepair (L228), describeMemoryConflict (L56)
mechanisms.limitations: A single JSON file on a local filesystem. It is not a general queue.
mechanisms.why: Idempotent, fenced claims keyed by state signature are exactly what ContextDB needs for background revalidation jobs: one revalidation per (item, frontier) and no repeated LLM checks of the same PENDING state. This is a ready-made design.

mechanisms.name: Pre-commit validation gate (read_only, frontmatter, size/depth/readOnlyFiles constraints)
mechanisms.how_it_works: A bash pre-commit hook is installed into every memory and shared repo. It runs Node to validate staged Markdown with validateMemoryFileFrontmatter. A description is required. read_only is protected: it cannot be added, changed or removed, and a file whose HEAD has read_only: true cannot be modified. memfs-v2 validates the whole staged tree. An optional .memfs.config.json adds maxFileCharacters, maxCoreMemoryCharacters, fileCharacterLimits globs, maxDepth, and readOnlyFiles globs that protect content, path and mode relative to HEAD. The validator runs as letta-memory-constraints.cjs. Post-turn sync runs invalidPendingMemory again before pushing.
mechanisms.evidence: letta-code/src/agent/memory-git-hooks.ts buildPreCommitHookScript (L38-184), installMemoryGitHooks (L294); src/memory-frontmatter.ts validateMemoryFileFrontmatter (L18-120); src/agent/memory-constraints.ts (validator script); src/memory-constraints.ts
mechanisms.limitations: It gates writes to memory, not agent actions in the world. Checks are syntactic and policy-level only, with no checks on content validity or dependencies. A client-side git hook can be bypassed with --no-verify, though the cloud remote presumably also validates (not visible in this repo).
mechanisms.why: Declarative write policies (protected fields, read-only globs, size budgets) checked at commit time are cheap, and users understand them. ContextDB can add a policy layer like this on revision commit, separate from its semantic validity machinery.

mechanisms.name: Tool-call gating: cross-agent memory guard, own-memory write allowance, PreToolUse hooks, kernel confinement
mechanisms.how_it_works: checkPermission step 0 is the cross-agent guard. It hard-denies in-process file tools (Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep/LS/ApplyPatch) whose resolved path lies under another agent's memory, allowing only self and an explicit parent; modes and rules cannot bypass this. isOwnMemoryWrite auto-approves Write/Edit/ApplyPatch only when every target, both as written and after resolving symlinks, lies within the agent's own memory roots. Memory subagents are kernel-sandboxed as whole processes and fail closed when no sandbox exists. User-configured PreToolUse hooks can block or rewrite tool input.
mechanisms.evidence: letta-code/src/permissions/cross-agent-guard.ts (header and resolveAllowedAgents), src/permissions/memory-write-allowance.ts isOwnMemoryWrite, src/memory-confinement.ts createMemoryConfinementLauncher, src/hooks/types.ts (PreToolUse 'can block them', updatedInput), src/hooks/executor.ts
mechanisms.limitations: Gating is by path and identity only. No action is checked against the freshness or validity of the context it was decided from, and there is no certificate concept.
mechanisms.why: PreToolUse with block or updatedInput is the natural insertion point for ContextDB's action-time certificate validation. A hook can send the certificate (the read set with revisions) to ContextDB and block if any pinned dependency is no longer valid. The path-scope ACL plus kernel confinement is a good default isolation model for multi-agent writers.

mechanisms.name: Shared memory via attached git repositories with permissions
mechanisms.how_it_works: The cloud API lists the extra repositories attached to an agent (GET /v1/agents/{id}/repositories, non-primary), each with permissions (read_write or other). Each one is cloned or mounted under the agent's tree (getRepositoryMountDir), synced in the background (syncAttachedAgentRepositories), and listed through a 5s TTL cache. Post-turn, a read_write repo is pushed with the same push, rebase-on-reject, push loop. A read-only repo with local edits or commits gets status push_failed. Several agents attached to the same repo share memory and skills (shared-memory-skills.ts discovers skills from them). The 'shared-memory' layout policy turns on v2 validation in the pre-commit hook.
mechanisms.evidence: letta-code/src/agent/attached-repositories.ts listAttachedAgentRepositories; src/agent/attached-repository-git-sync.ts syncPendingAttachedRepositoryCommitsUnlocked, syncPendingAttachedRepositoryCommitsAfterTurn; src/agent/memory-git.ts syncAttachedAgentRepositories (L1421), syncRepoMount; src/agent/shared-memory-skills.ts; memory-git-hooks.ts installSharedMemoryPreCommitHook
mechanisms.readme_vs_code: implemented (client side); server-side ACL enforcement is not in this repo
mechanisms.limitations: Sharing is coarse: a whole repo, eventually consistent, and refreshed only at turn boundaries. Agents get no notification of other agents' changes until they pull. There is no subscription per item and no consistency guarantee beyond git ancestry.
mechanisms.why: It confirms that users want 'shared scratchpad repos with rw/ro grants attached to several agents'. ContextDB's namespaces with ACLs plus push notifications per item (instead of turn-boundary pulls) are a direct upgrade.

mechanisms.name: (Retired V1) shared block fan-out: rebuild prompts of all attached agents on change
mechanisms.how_it_works: A block is one DB row attached to N agents through blocks_agents. update_block_async computes has_prompt_changes over PROMPT_AFFECTING_BLOCK_FIELDS = {description,label,limit,read_only,value} and skips no-op updates. After commit it calls _rebuild_system_prompts_for_connected_agents. That function looks up the agent ids for the block and runs rebuild_system_prompt_async(force=True) for each. The rebuild recompiles memory and skips if the compiled string is already in the system message and force is not set.
mechanisms.evidence: letta-archive/letta/services/block_manager.py PROMPT_AFFECTING_BLOCK_FIELDS (L32), _rebuild_system_prompts_for_connected_agents (L61-67), update_block_async (L211-270); letta/services/agent_manager.py rebuild_system_prompt_async (~L1523-1565); letta/orm/blocks_agents.py
mechanisms.limitations: Fan-out is one hop only (block to agent prompt). Rebuilds are eager and synchronous, and failures are only logged. Decisions derived from the block are not tracked. The approach was retired in favour of git MemFS.
mechanisms.why: This is the reverse index item-to-consumer with one-hop eager invalidation. ContextDB generalises it to a transitive DAG. The idea of a 'prompt-affecting field set' filter, so that metadata-only changes do not invalidate anything, is worth copying.

mechanisms.name: (Retired V1) optimistic-lock version column + linear undo/redo history
mechanisms.how_it_works: Block has version_id_col=version (SQLAlchemy versioning). An UPDATE carries WHERE version=loaded and raises StaleDataError, mapped to ConcurrentUpdateError. checkpoint_block_async copies the block state into block_history with sequence_number = current+1 (unique on block_id+seq), records actor_type and actor_id, deletes 'future' entries beyond the current pointer (so history is strictly linear), and moves current_history_entry_id. undo/redo move to seq-1/seq+1 through _move_block_to_sequence. Deadlocks retry with exponential backoff.
mechanisms.evidence: letta-archive/letta/orm/block.py L53-61; letta/orm/block_history.py; letta/services/block_manager.py checkpoint_block_async (L842-911), undo_checkpoint_block (L952), redo_checkpoint_block (L1004); letta/orm/sqlalchemy_base.py update_async StaleDataError handling (~L779)
mechanisms.limitations: The version is not exposed in the public BlockUpdate schema, so clients cannot send an expected version: the CAS protects only the read-modify-write inside one server request. History is truncated on a new checkpoint after undo, which is destructive. There are no branches.
mechanisms.why: Shows what not to do. ContextDB must expose expected_rev to callers, because agents read in one turn and write in a later one, and must keep history append-only, never truncating 'future' revisions. Letta itself retired this design.

mechanisms.name: Projection-based context packing (core vs deferred memory, budgets)
mechanisms.how_it_works: In memfs-v2, only the root MEMORY.md and the projected child */MEMORY.md indexes are read into the prompt. Other files appear as a tree with descriptions only (<deferred-memory>), and the agent reads them on demand with the memory/Read tool. maxCoreMemoryCharacters caps the inline portion. memfs-v1 renders system/ files in full and the rest as a tree.
mechanisms.evidence: letta-code/src/backend/local/system-prompt-compilation.ts collectCommittedMemoryFiles (shouldRead logic), renderRootMemoryProjection (L154), renderMemfsProjection (L305); src/tools/impl/memory.ts renderDirectory/renderFile
mechanisms.limitations: Selection is by path convention, not relevance or dependency. There is no record of which deferred files the agent actually read in a turn.
mechanisms.why: A two-tier context (pinned core plus an index of descriptions read lazily) is a good default packing policy. ContextDB should additionally log lazy reads into the read certificate, which Letta does not do.

mechanisms.name: Commit authorship as provenance; wiki-links for display only
mechanisms.how_it_works: Provenance is the git author: the agent id and name are set in user.name/email and letta.agentId local config. Commit messages give the reason, and merge messages summarise the reflection commit subjects (buildReflectionMergeMessage). [[wiki-links]] between memory files are extracted only when the UI asks for include_references, to draw a graph. They are never used for invalidation.
mechanisms.evidence: letta-code/src/agent/memory-git.ts commitMemoryPaths, prepareLocalOnlyMemoryRepoForGitOps, ensureLocalMemfsGitConfig; src/agent/memory-worktree.ts buildReflectionMergeMessage (L94); src/websocket/listener/commands/memory.ts extractMemoryReferences (~L291)
mechanisms.limitations: There are no typed dependencies, no justification records, and no derivation links from conclusions to sources. Links are untyped text references.
mechanisms.why: No dependency/justification mechanism exists to borrow. The only lesson is that agents naturally write [[links]], which ContextDB could ingest as a low-confidence Ref-type dependency hint.

mechanisms.name: App Server websocket memory protocol + memory_updated push
mechanisms.how_it_works: Typed request/response commands: memory_history (git log optionally per file, limit), memory_file_at_ref (read path@SHA), memory_commit_diff, read/write memory file, and a listing with include_references. After writes, the server pushes {type:'memory_updated', affected_paths, timestamp} so UIs refresh. conversation_recompile forces a prompt rebuild.
mechanisms.evidence: letta-code/src/types/protocol_v2.ts (L1005-1210 MemoryHistoryCommand, MemoryFileAtRefCommand, MemoryUpdatedMessage, conversation_recompile L1608); src/websocket/listener/commands/memory.ts (~L453, L868); src/websocket/listener/turn-cleanup.ts L65
mechanisms.limitations: The push events go to UIs, not to other agents. There is no MCP server exposing memory, and no subscription by item or predicate.
mechanisms.why: An affected_paths change-feed plus point-in-time reads (path@rev) is a minimal, proven API shape. ContextDB should expose the equivalent (subscribe(items) leading to changed or invalidated events, read(item@rev)) over both MCP and a websocket.

analysis.overlap_with_contextdb:
Little overlap with ContextDB's core semantics.
- Dependency-driven transitive invalidation: NONE. Current letta-code detects staleness only as "memory repo HEAD SHA changed", and only at turn start (local-backend.ts getOrCompileSystemPrompt). Retired V1 had one-hop fan-out from a changed shared block to the prompts of its attached agents (block_manager.py _rebuild_system_prompts_for_connected_agents). Neither tracks which beliefs or decisions depend on which items, and neither propagates further.
- AND/OR justification, support counting, alternatives: NONE. Wiki-links are display-only.
- Structural vs semantic validity / PENDING: NONE. Conflicts are textual git conflicts. Typed sync statuses (dirty/conflict/invalid/push_failed) exist only as operational states.
- CAS: the remote git branch tip acts as a global CAS register (non-fast-forward rejection, then rebase). V1 had a server-internal optimistic version column that clients could not supply. No per-item expected-revision CAS is exposed.
- Action gating: path/identity ACLs (cross-agent guard, own-memory write allowance, kernel confinement), pre-commit policy validation, and generic PreToolUse hooks that can block. Nothing checks an action against the validity of the context it was based on, and there are no certificates.
- Certified reads: partial. The compiled context records the memfs revision it was built from and compares it before reuse, which is a whole-repo pin rather than a per-dependency read set.
- Multi-agent sharing: yes, coarse. Attached git repos with rw/ro permissions, worktree branches for background writers, merge or abort with typed outcomes.
analysis.could_contextdb_be_built_as_plugin_on_it:
Not as a core: the git-file substrate has no item-level heads, typed dependency edges or justification graph, and whole-repo SHAs are too coarse for ContextDB's semantics. As an integration target, yes. letta-code offers three usable seams.
1. An MCP client (src/mcp-client.ts), so a ContextDB MCP server can provide certified read/write tools to Letta agents.
2. PreToolUse hooks that can block or rewrite tool input (src/hooks/types.ts, executor.ts). These are the natural place for action-time certificate validation: send the read set with revisions, block when a dependency is invalid or PENDING.
3. Post-commit/pre-commit hooks on the MemFS repo (memory-git-hooks.ts). These could mirror each memory commit into ContextDB as new revisions (git SHA as the Pin source revision), with the [[links]] and reflection-merge messages as weak provenance hints.

A practical product path is a "ContextDB adapter for git-backed agent memory". It would ingest MemFS commits, keep the dependency DAG and validity state, and send invalidation back through a <memory_update>-style mid-conversation delta (as in local-backend.ts formatMidConversationMemoryUpdate) and a memory_updated-style change feed. Letta's archive README/AGENTS.md says the retired V1 server should not be used or copied; only design ideas from it are cited here.

verification.overlap_verdict: Confirmed, with small refinements. (1) No transitive dependency invalidation and no AND/OR justification, support counting, or PENDING state exist. [[links]] are parsed only for UI graph display (include_references), and typed sync statuses are operational only. (2) CAS: confirmed. The remote branch tip acts as a global CAS register (non-fast-forward, then pull --rebase, then push). The V1 Block ORM has an internal SQLAlchemy version_id_col ('Optimistic locking version counter') that the Pydantic schema does not expose. No per-item expected-revision CAS exists. (3) Certified reads are partial, and only in LocalBackend: the pin is the whole-repo HEAD SHA plus rawSystemHash, checked when the next turn starts. Refinement: the memory repo can be pulled or rebased between turns, so a staleness check against HEAD at turn start can miss remote changes not yet pulled. (4) Action gating is path/identity only: the cross-agent guard applies to in-process tools, shells are unconfined by default, the guard can be disabled with a parent flag, and PreToolUse hooks can block or rewrite. No certificate concept exists. (5) Multi-agent sharing is coarse and confirmed: attached repos with permissions; read-only repos are enforced client-side as push_failed. One refinement: memory-worker integration is weaker than reflection finalize (no parent-dirty check and no origin refresh). Overall, 'little overlap with ContextDB core semantics' is accurate. Letta's proven contributions are operational: git-backed immutable revisions, branch-and-merge with typed outcomes for background writers, a liveness-fenced lease, token-fenced idempotent repair claims, commit-time policy gates, a revision-pinned prompt with a delta message that keeps the prompt cache, and an affected_paths change feed.

analysis.one_line_summary: A MySQL-compatible SQL database with Git semantics. Data lives in content-addressed prolly trees, commits form a Merkle DAG, and branches are named refs updated by a root-level compare-and-swap. Merges are 3-way at row and cell level, and conflicts and violations are stored as artifacts. Dolt has no notion of dependencies, justification, or semantic invalidation.
analysis.architecture:
Written in Go and licensed Apache-2.0. Layers, bottom to top:
(1) ChunkStore (go/store/chunks/chunk_store.go): content-addressed chunks keyed by 20-byte hashes, plus a single mutable root hash. Root(ctx) reads it and Commit(ctx, current, last) swaps it (CAS). The storage format is NBS table files (go/store/nbs), with GC.
(2) Prolly trees (go/store/prolly, go/store/prolly/tree): sorted key/value maps with content-defined chunking (node_splitter.go: rollingHashSplitter, keySplitter, weibullCheck). The same content always produces the same tree shape and hashes, whatever order it was written in. That makes structural sharing, an O(diff) diff (diff.go skipCommon/skipCommonParents skip equal subtrees by hash) and a 3-way merge (merge.go ThreeWayMerge, three_way_differ.go ThreeWayDiffer) possible.
(3) The datas layer (go/store/datas): the store root is a flatbuffer "storeroot" holding an AddressMap from dataset id (refs/heads/x, workingSets/heads/x, tags, stash) to a head hash. The Commit flatbuffer (go/serial/commit.fbs) has root, height, parent_addrs, parent_closure (a prolly map of every ancestor, used for fast merge-base and ancestry checks), name/email/description/timestamps and a signature. A WorkingSet (workingset.go workingset_flatbuffer) holds the working root, the staged root, and optional MergeState/RebaseState.
(4) doltcore (go/libraries/doltcore): RootValue (tables to prolly maps), merge (merge.go, merge_prolly_rows.go), commitgraph (merge_bases.go GetMergeBases), branch_control (per-branch ACLs), and the SQL engine integration in sqle/dsess (transactions.go DoltTransaction).
Processes: a dolt CLI, or `dolt sql-server` (MySQL wire protocol) where many clients share one process. Version control is exposed as SQL stored procedures and system tables (dolt_commit, dolt_merge, dolt_branch, dolt_diff, dolt_history, dolt_conflicts, dolt_constraint_violations, AS OF queries).
MCP: cmd/dolt/commands/sqlserver/mcp.go (mcpRun, registerMCPService) embeds the external module github.com/dolthub/dolt-mcp (NewMCPHTTPServer, toolsets.PrimitiveToolSetV1) as an HTTP MCP server. It talks to the sql-server as a configured SQL user. The tool definitions are in that external module, which I did not read.

mechanisms.name: Immutable content-addressed commits + named refs (dataset heads)
mechanisms.how_it_works: Every value (table map, root value, commit) is an immutable chunk addressed by its hash. A branch is just an entry dataset_id -> commit hash in the store-root AddressMap. A commit records root hash, parent hashes, height, a parent_closure map and author metadata. 'Superseding' means writing a new commit whose parents include the old head and moving the ref. Old versions stay reachable by hash until GC. BuildNewCommit requires the current head to be among opts.Parents unless Force is set, otherwise it returns ErrMergeNeeded. Amend requires the head to equal AmendedCommit.
mechanisms.evidence: go/store/datas/database_common.go BuildNewCommit (~L522-547), hasParentHash; go/serial/commit.fbs table Commit; go/store/datas/commit.go newCommitForValue; go/store/datas/commit_closure.go writeFbCommitParentClosure
mechanisms.limitations: Versioning is per database root (whole snapshot), not per item. There is no per-row revision chain. Row history comes from walking commits (dolt_history), not from per-item 'supersedes' links. Supersession is positional (newer commit), not semantic.
mechanisms.why: This matches ContextDB's immutable revisions + logical heads. Borrow it directly: content-hash revisions, a head map from logical id to revision hash, and parent pointers. A parent_closure-style ancestor index gives cheap 'is A an ancestor of B' checks for certificates.

mechanisms.name: Single-root optimistic CAS with retry-on-conflict and per-dataset preconditions
mechanisms.how_it_works: database.update() loops through these steps: read root hash; load the datasets AddressMap; apply editFB; write a new storeroot chunk; call ChunkStore.Commit(new, old). If that returns false it gets ErrOptimisticLockFailed and goes round again. CommitDatasets atomically updates N datasets in one root swap. Each update carries datasetCommitPrecondition{DatasetID, ExpectedHead, NotEqual, OnFailure}. These are re-checked against the freshly loaded map on every retry, so a mismatch yields ErrOptimisticLockFailed or the custom error. SetHead also accepts Precondition funcs that are re-validated before each CAS attempt. Deleting a branch checks the head is unchanged and the working set is clean (ErrDirtyWorkspace).
mechanisms.evidence: go/store/datas/database_common.go update() (~L767-809), tryCommitChunks (~L902), CommitDatasets (~L689-760), Precondition type (~L202-209), doDelete (~L811); go/store/datas/dataset_updates.go datasetCommitPrecondition; go/store/chunks/chunk_store.go Root/Commit (~L111-116)
mechanisms.limitations: There is one global root, so every ref update in the DB contends on the same CAS (it is serialized, which is fine at agent scale). Preconditions only compare head hashes, not read sets.
mechanisms.why: This is the multi-head atomic CAS ContextDB needs. Commit several logical heads at once, with ExpectedHead preconditions per head, and re-validate on retry. The Precondition-func hook, re-run before each CAS, is a good place to re-validate an action certificate's read set atomically with the write.

mechanisms.name: SQL transaction commit = merge-on-conflict with bounded retries
mechanisms.how_it_works: DoltTransaction.commitHeads takes a per-branch TxLock, then makes up to maxTxCommitRetries=5 attempts. It resolves the current working set. If it changed since the transaction started (workingAndStagedEqual false), it 3-way merges txStart (base), existing (theirs) and ours via merge.MergeRoots (tx.mergeRoots). It then validates there are no unresolved conflicts or constraint violations (validateWorkingSetForCommit, unless the dolt_allow_commit_conflicts or dolt_force_transaction_commit flags are set). Finally it calls CommitHeadUpdates with PrevHash/ExpectedHead preconditions, and retries on ErrOptimisticLockFailed/ErrMergeNeeded. Conflicts that cannot be merged roll back with ErrUnresolvedConflictsCommit or a deadlock-style retry error.
mechanisms.evidence: go/libraries/doltcore/sqle/dsess/transactions.go commitHeads (~L341-520), mergeRoots (~L524), prepareDoltCommit (~L172-260), validateWorkingSetForCommit (~L646), ErrRetryTransaction
mechanisms.limitations: The merge is structural only. Two writes that don't touch the same cells but are semantically incompatible merge cleanly. Only constraint checks (FK/unique/check/null) catch some of these.
mechanisms.why: This is a good model for concurrent agent writes: auto-merge disjoint edits and reject or retry overlapping ones. ContextDB should add one thing: after the structural merge, run justification and dependency re-validation and mark affected items PENDING. Dolt only checks constraints.

mechanisms.name: Branches, working sets, merge-base (git merge-base --all)
mechanisms.how_it_works: Each branch has a head ref plus a workingSets/<branch> entry (working root, staged root, MergeState). GetMergeBases walks both sides with flags, as git does, and returns every best common ancestor. It can use an AncestryIndex (the parent closure) to walk only one side. GetCommitAncestor picks the tallest one, ties broken by hash. Ghost commits (shallow history) give a GhostCommitError.
mechanisms.evidence: go/libraries/doltcore/commitgraph/merge_bases.go GetMergeBases, walkBothSides; go/libraries/doltcore/doltdb/commit.go GetCommitAncestor/GetCommitAncestors (~L160-200); go/libraries/doltcore/merge/merge_base.go MergeBase/MergeBases; go/store/datas/workingset.go workingset_flatbuffer, NewMergeState
mechanisms.limitations: Branches are whole-DB forks. There is no partial or scoped branch over a subset of items.
mechanisms.why: For what-if/alternatives: a ContextDB 'alternative' can be a branch (a new head namespace forked from a revision) that is cheap because of structural sharing. Merging an alternative back uses merge-base + 3-way. ContextDB likely wants scoped branches (a subset of logical ids) rather than whole-DB forks.

mechanisms.name: Row- and cell-level 3-way merge with classified diff ops
mechanisms.how_it_works: ThreeWayDiffer zips the two diff streams base->left and base->right (both prolly diffs) by key. One-sided edits become LeftAdd/Modify/Delete or RightAdd/Modify/Delete. Identical edits are Convergent. Different edits to the same key call resolveCb = valueMerger.TryMerge, which merges column by column (processBaseColumn/processColumn): if only one side changed a column against base, take it; if both changed it to equal values, take either (ties broken by byte order); otherwise it is a conflict. A delete against a modify conflicts only if the modified side actually changed a value. A pluggable RowMergePolicy can return Defer/Resolved/Conflict per row before the default. JSON columns get a 3-way JSON merge (MergeJSON, three_way_json_differ.go).
mechanisms.evidence: go/store/prolly/tree/three_way_differ.go ThreeWayDiffer.Next (dsMatch case ~L232-268), DiffOp enum (~L297-313), RowMergePolicy/RunRowMergePolicy (~L49-90); go/libraries/doltcore/merge/merge_prolly_rows.go valueMerger.TryMerge (~L2048), processBaseColumn (~L2098), processColumn (~L2200), MergeJSON (~L2431), treeRowMergePolicy (~L575)
mechanisms.limitations: Conflict means a syntactic overlap on the same cell. There are no semantic merge rules beyond the pluggable policy hook.
mechanisms.why: The DiffOp taxonomy (one-sided, convergent, divergent-resolved, divergent-conflict, delete-conflict) and the per-field 3-way rule are directly reusable for merging item revisions across agent branches. The RowMergePolicy hook is where type-specific merge rules go, such as CRDT-like sets for evidence lists.

mechanisms.name: Conflicts and constraint violations persisted as 'artifacts' that block commit
mechanisms.how_it_works: A merge writes conflicts and constraint violations into a per-table ArtifactMap (a prolly map). The key is the source row key + commit hash + artifact type + a violation-info hash. ArtifactType is one of Conflict, ForeignKeyViol, UniqueKeyViol, ChkConsViol, NullViol. Validators (checkValidator, uniqValidator, nullValidator) run over each ThreeWayDiff during the merge and insert or clear artifacts. They surface as dolt_conflicts and dolt_constraint_violations tables. A transaction commit is refused while they exist, unless an override flag is set.
mechanisms.evidence: go/store/prolly/artifact_map.go ArtifactType consts (~L36-48), ArtifactMap; go/libraries/doltcore/merge/merge_prolly_rows.go newCheckValidator/validateDiff, uniqValidator, nullValidator, conflictMerger (~L1342-1410), mergeTableArtifacts (~L1912); go/libraries/doltcore/sqle/dsess/transactions.go validateWorkingSetForCommit
mechanisms.limitations: Artifacts are created only at merge time. There is no ongoing staleness tracking and no propagation to dependents.
mechanisms.why: This is close to ContextDB's 'PENDING not FALSE': unresolved items are stored as first-class, versioned records and a commit or action gate refuses while they exist. ContextDB can model PENDING validations, conflicts between alternatives, and violated invariants as artifacts keyed by (item, revision, type).

mechanisms.name: Prolly trees: history-independent content-defined chunking
mechanisms.how_it_works: Node boundaries come from a rolling hash over items (rollingHashSplitter, with a Weibull size distribution) or from a hash of the key (keySplitter). Identical content therefore always gives identical node hashes whatever the edit history. Diff walks two trees and skips any subtree with an equal hash (skipCommon/skipCommonParents), so the cost grows with the size of the change. Patches can be applied directly (tree_patcher.go, merge.go ThreeWayMerge/SendPatches).
mechanisms.evidence: go/store/prolly/tree/node_splitter.go rollingHashSplitter, keySplitter, weibullCheck, DeterministicHashLevel; go/store/prolly/tree/diff.go skipCommon (~L251), skipCommonParents (~L290); go/store/prolly/tree/merge.go ThreeWayMerge (~L64)
mechanisms.limitations: Complex to implement and tune. It only pays off for large maps. A ContextDB with thousands to low millions of items could get similar benefits from a simpler Merkle/HAMT, or by relying on SQLite plus per-revision rows.
mechanisms.why: Cheap snapshots and O(diff) branch comparison make many what-if branches affordable. Use it as a library idea or embed Dolt, rather than reimplementing it in v1.

mechanisms.name: Commit hooks (post-commit, replication) and branch ACLs
mechanisms.how_it_works: CommitHook.Execute(ctx, ds, db) runs after a dataset head update (it is used for replication and push-on-write) and can return an async wait func. It is read-only and post-hoc: it cannot veto the write. branch_control.CheckAccessForBranch enforces per-(user, host, db, branch) Write/Admin permissions, checked by SQL operations.
mechanisms.evidence: go/libraries/doltcore/doltdb/hooksdatabase.go CommitHook interface (~L67-90); go/libraries/doltcore/branch_control/branch_control.go CheckAccess (~L235), CheckAccessForBranch (~L249)
mechanisms.limitations: Dolt has no pre-action certificate validation and no external-action gating. Hooks run after the commit, and ACLs only check identity and branch.
mechanisms.why: Per-branch ACLs map onto per-agent write scopes. ContextDB's action-time certificate check has to be built itself, ideally as a datas-style Precondition re-checked inside the CAS loop.

mechanisms.name: SQL-first VCS API + embedded MCP server
mechanisms.how_it_works: Version control is exposed through SQL procedures and system tables over the MySQL wire protocol (dolt sql-server). It also optionally starts an HTTP MCP server from the external dolthub/dolt-mcp module (PrimitiveToolSetV1), which connects back as a configured SQL user.
mechanisms.evidence: go/cmd/dolt/commands/sqlserver/mcp.go mcpInit, mcpRun (NewMCPHTTPServer, toolsets.WithToolSet(&toolsets.PrimitiveToolSetV1{})), registerMCPService; go/cmd/dolt/commands/sqlserver/mcp_validate.go
mechanisms.readme_vs_code: partially (MCP wiring is implemented in this repo; the tool definitions live in the external dolt-mcp module, which I did not read)
mechanisms.limitations: The MCP tools are generic SQL/VCS primitives, not context- or justification-aware.
mechanisms.why: Shows a workable pattern: expose branch/merge/diff as both SQL and MCP tools from one server process. ContextDB could put its own MCP layer on top of a Dolt sql-server.

mechanisms.name: Provenance = commit metadata only; no dependency links
mechanisms.how_it_works: Each commit carries name, email, description, timestamps and an optional signature. Lineage is the parent DAG. There are no per-row provenance fields, no typed dependencies between rows, and no justification graph. Foreign keys are the only cross-row relation, and they are checked as constraints at write and merge time.
mechanisms.evidence: go/serial/commit.fbs table Commit; FK checking in go/libraries/doltcore/merge/violations_fk_prolly.go
mechanisms.readme_vs_code: implemented (provenance is limited to commits); dependency tracking does not exist
mechanisms.limitations: Changing upstream data cannot transitively invalidate anything.
mechanisms.why: ContextDB's AND/OR justification DAG, Pin/Cur/Sem/Ref typed dependencies, and flip-only propagation must be built entirely on top. Dolt offers nothing here beyond FK constraints.

analysis.overlap_with_contextdb:
Dolt overlaps with ContextDB on: immutable content-addressed revisions; logical heads (refs) moved by an atomic multi-ref CAS with expected-head preconditions re-checked on retry; branching for what-if/alternatives with cheap structural sharing; row- and cell-level 3-way merge with a clear conflict taxonomy; and conflicts and violations persisted as versioned artifacts that block commits.

Dolt does NOT do:
- dependency-driven transitive invalidation: no dependency graph, no support counting, no propagation. FK constraints are the only cross-row relation, and they are checked, not propagated.
- justification (AND/OR) or alternative support: branches are whole-DB forks, not justified alternatives.
- Pin/Cur/Sem/Ref typed dependencies.
- semantic validity or PENDING states, beyond merge-time conflict and violation artifacts.
- certified reads or action-time certificate validation: CommitHooks run after the commit and cannot veto, and branch_control only checks identity per branch.

Nuances: (1) locks are taken on every involved working set, sorted to avoid deadlock, so this is not a single per-branch lock. (2) The override flags (dolt_allow_commit_conflicts / dolt_force_transaction_commit) apply only to conflicts that were already present in the transaction's own state (the fast-forward case). Conflicts produced by the transaction-vs-transaction merge are always rolled back with ErrRetryTransaction wrapped as sql.ErrLockDeadlock, whatever the flags. Force covers constraint violations in both cases. (3) An amend that loses the race returns a retry error immediately instead of looping. (4) After 5 failed attempts the result is ErrOptimisticLockFailed.

verification.overlap_verdict: Confirmed, with two corrections. (1) Atomic multi-ref CAS (CommitDatasets) supports only head-hash equality and inequality preconditions. Arbitrary validation callbacks (Precondition funcs) exist only on single-dataset SetHead. Dolt therefore has multi-head CAS and per-head validation hooks, but not the two together, which ContextDB would need for checking a certificate's read set during a multi-head commit. (2) Merge-time conflict artifacts block a transaction commit unless override flags are set, and those flags only cover conflicts already present in the transaction's own state. Conflicts produced by the transaction-vs-transaction merge always roll back as retry errors. The 'Dolt does NOT do' list holds against the source. I found no dependency graph, support counting, propagation, justification, typed dependencies, PENDING state or pre-commit veto hook. CommitHook errors are explicitly ignored by the caller. Branch ACLs gate by user/host/db/branch and permission level (Admin/Write/Merge/Read).

analysis.one_line_summary: ai-memory is a Rust, SQLite plus markdown-wiki memory server for coding CLIs. It gives you immutable page versions with an is_latest head and supersedes chain, an optional expected_page_id CAS on write and delete, claim-once handoff batons, bi-temporal as_of windows, page_evidence provenance, and contradiction edges that only feed lint and ranking. mcp-memory-service is a Python vector-memory MCP server with parent_id/superseded_by lineage, a guarded supersede UPDATE, write-time contradiction flagging by embedding similarity and text divergence, and HLC event-log sync. Neither does dependency-driven invalidation, PENDING semantics, or action gating.
analysis.architecture: ai-memory: a Rust 2024 cargo workspace in crates/: ai-memory-core (types: Page, Relation, Handoff), ai-memory-store (SQLite via rusqlite, 83 refinery migrations in crates/ai-memory-store/migrations, FTS5 plus optional embeddings, one writer thread), ai-memory-wiki (markdown files are the source of truth, git checkpoints, HTTP admission webhook chain, a mutation_lock RwLock), ai-memory-mcp (rmcp MCP server in server.rs), ai-memory-consolidate (LLM consolidator, lint, dream merge, decay sweep), plus hooks, CLI and web. Process model: one server, many harness clients over MCP/HTTP with hook-driven session capture. All mutations go through a dedicated writer OS thread fed by an mpsc channel (crates/ai-memory-store/src/writer.rs header, WriteCmd enum), and reads use separate connections. Data model: workspaces > projects > pages(id, path, body_sha256, is_latest, supersedes, valid_from/valid_to, superseded_at tombstone, expires_at, salience, author_id), links(from_page_id, to_page_id, to_path, link_type in references|causes|fixes|contradicts), entities with entity_page_links(valid_from, superseded_at), page_evidence, page_feedback, sessions, observations, handoffs, agent_messages, audit_log. MCP tools: memory_query (supports as_of and include_superseded), memory_recent, memory_feedback, memory_forget_sweep, memory_lint, memory_consolidate, memory_auto_improve, memory_write_page (expected_page_id or create_only), memory_read_page, memory_read_session_observations, memory_restore_page, memory_delete_page (expected_page_id), memory_handoff_begin/list/accept/cancel, memory_message_send/list/pop/cancel, memory_status, memory_briefing, memory_explore, memory_install_self_routing. mcp-memory-service: Python with many storage backends (sqlite_vec built from mixins in storage/mixins/*.py, plus hybrid, cloudflare, milvus, remote_http). Data model: memories(content_hash PK-like, content, tags CSV, memory_type, metadata JSON, parent_id, version, confidence, superseded_by, deleted_at), memory_graph(source_hash, target_hash, relationship_type in causes|fixes|contradicts|supports|follows|related), beliefs(status candidate|active|disputed|superseded, derived_from, contradicted_by JSON), sync_events (append-only, HLC). MCP tools are in tools/registry.py: memory_store, memory_search, memory_update, memory_delete, memory_conflicts, memory_resolve, memory_graph, memory_consolidate, memory_quality, mistake_note_*, and others.

mechanisms.name: ai-memory immutable page versions with an is_latest head per path
mechanisms.how_it_works: pages rows are never edited in place for content. upsert_page_in_tx hashes the body (sha256) and loads the current is_latest=1 row for (workspace, project, path). If body, frontmatter (ignoring generated.at), title, tier and pinned all match, nothing is written: it is a no-op that only records evidence. Otherwise, in one transaction it sets the old row to is_latest=0 with valid_to=now, closes that row's entity_page_links windows (superseded_at=now), inserts a new row with supersedes=old.id and valid_from=now, rebuilds the new row's outgoing links, re-points incoming links to the new id, records evidence and audits 'supersede_page'. A partial unique index idx_pages_latest_path ... WHERE is_latest=1 guarantees one head per path. Writing to a tombstoned path re-links the new version onto the old chain ('resurrect_tombstoned_page').
mechanisms.evidence: crates/ai-memory-store/src/ops.rs upsert_page (l.198), upsert_page_in_tx (l.1810-2030), most_recent_tombstone_at_path; migrations V01__init.sql (pages, idx_pages_latest_path), V03__decay.sql, V62__page_ingestion_windows.sql
mechanisms.limitations: The head is keyed by file path, not by logical entity id. Versions form a linear chain per path, so there is no first-class branching or alternatives. The 'concurrent loser stays reachable' guarantee holds only because the losing write becomes an older version in the chain; it is not a fork.
mechanisms.why: This maps directly onto ContextDB's immutable revisions plus logical heads. The partial-unique-index trick (one is_latest per key) and the content-hash no-op short-circuit are cheap and proven.

mechanisms.name: ai-memory expected_page_id / create_only CAS on write and delete
mechanisms.how_it_works: Callers may pass expected_page_id (meaning the head must still be this version) or create_only (meaning no head may exist). page_precondition() turns these into PagePrecondition::Latest(id) or ::Absent. ops::upsert_page_if reads the current head inside the same SQLite transaction as the write and returns ConditionalUpsert::Mismatch{current} without writing when the precondition fails. The MCP layer turns a mismatch into a precondition_failed error whose data carries the expected and current ids, so the client can re-read and retry. The delete path pre-checks, then re-checks under the wiki mutation_lock write guard and inside the delete transaction (delete_page_if_latest).
mechanisms.evidence: crates/ai-memory-store/src/ops.rs PagePrecondition, ConditionalUpsert, upsert_page_if (l.257-314); crates/ai-memory-mcp/src/server.rs page_precondition (~l.7190), precondition_failed, memory_delete_page (l.5284-5430); crates/ai-memory-wiki/src/wiki.rs precondition_holds (l.3678), mutation_lock (l.193)
mechanisms.limitations: The CAS is optional: plain writes are last-writer-becomes-head with no conflict signal. It covers a single key only, with no multi-key or transactional read-set validation. Nothing checks read dependencies of other items.
mechanisms.why: This is exactly the head-CAS primitive ContextDB needs, and the error shape (expected vs current) is a good API pattern. ContextDB should make the CAS mandatory for agent writes and extend it to a read-set or certificate.

mechanisms.name: Single-writer actor thread plus a wiki mutation RwLock
mechanisms.how_it_works: All mutating SQL goes over an mpsc channel to one OS thread that owns the writer rusqlite::Connection, and each command replies on a oneshot. This removes SQLITE_BUSY by construction. The wiki layer adds an async RwLock (mutation_lock) around file rename plus DB upsert so the markdown file and the row stay in step. Pages are shared across all sessions and users in a project (author_id is attribution only, never a read filter), and handoffs are owner-scoped.
mechanisms.evidence: crates/ai-memory-store/src/writer.rs module doc l.1-8, enum WriteCmd, upsert_page_if l.2799/3881; crates/ai-memory-wiki/src/wiki.rs mutation_lock usages l.528-1114; AGENTS.md invariant #16 (l.491-515)
mechanisms.limitations: Single process and single node. Each write is serialized, but nothing gives snapshot-consistent multi-item reads to agents.
mechanisms.why: This is a simple, proven way to get serializable writes on embedded SQLite for a local multi-agent daemon. It is a good starting point for ContextDB's writer before any distribution.

mechanisms.name: Claim-once handoff baton (open -> accepted CAS) and the agent_messages inbox
mechanisms.how_it_works: A handoff (summary, open_questions, next_steps, files_touched) is written on SessionEnd or by memory_handoff_begin. accept_handoff_in_transaction validates that the receiver session exists, matches scope and agent, and is open, then runs UPDATE handoffs SET state='accepted' ... WHERE id=? AND state='open' [AND owner clause]. Only the one racing session that changes a row wins. On accept, expire_superseded_auto_handoffs expires older open auto-handoffs for the same cwd and owner. agent_messages follows the same state machine (pending -> claimed or cancelled), and claimed or cancelled rows are kept for audit.
mechanisms.evidence: crates/ai-memory-store/src/ops.rs accept_handoff_in_transaction (l.4582-4800, UPDATE at ~l.4724), expire_superseded_auto_handoffs (l.4823), expire_open_handoffs, cancel_handoff, pop_message_in_transaction (l.5184); migrations V02__handoffs.sql, V39__handoff_ownership.sql, V64__agent_messages.sql
mechanisms.limitations: The handoff is free-text state with no structured dependencies, and nothing checks that the handoff's claims still hold when it is accepted.
mechanisms.why: A claim-once state CAS suits task or lease handoff between agents. ContextDB could attach a context certificate to a handoff and re-validate it on accept.

mechanisms.name: Bi-temporal-lite as_of windows (page and entity-link grain)
mechanisms.how_it_works: Each page version carries valid_from (its created_at) and valid_to (the successor's created_at, or the tombstone time). entity_page_links carry valid_from and superseded_at. memory_query with as_of filters with valid_from <= t AND (valid_to IS NULL OR valid_to > t), and the reader's latest_only(table, include_superseded) switches between head-only and audit modes. Windows close in the same transaction as the supersede. Migrations V58 and V62 fixed windows that stayed open after successor-less retirements.
mechanisms.evidence: migrations V56__entity_link_validity.sql, V58__close_retired_entity_windows.sql, V62__page_ingestion_windows.sql; ops.rs upsert_page_in_tx window closes, backfill_page_windows_in_batches (l.1719); crates/ai-memory-store/src/reader.rs latest_only (l.64), entity-window predicates (~l.5864-5880); server.rs test memory_query_as_of_travels_the_entity_timeline
mechanisms.limitations: These are ingestion-time (transaction-time) windows only. There is no valid-time separate from when a fact was written.
mechanisms.why: ContextDB revisions need time-travel reads for audit and for re-checking certificates against a past snapshot. The lessons on closing windows on every retirement path, and on chunked backfills, transfer directly.

mechanisms.name: Typed links that follow the head (references/causes/fixes/contradicts)
mechanisms.how_it_works: Links come from the page body ([[path]], [[project:path]]) and the frontmatter relations: map. replace_links_in_tx deletes and re-inserts a version's outgoing links on every write. Each link stores to_path and a resolved to_page_id. refresh_incoming_links_for_path re-points to_page_id of every incoming link (same-project, cross-project and _global) to the new head when a target is superseded. So a link is always a 'current' dependency (like ContextDB Cur), never pinned to a version. dangling_cross_project_links feeds lint.
mechanisms.evidence: crates/ai-memory-core/src/page.rs enum Relation (l.513-546), LinkTarget; ops.rs replace_links_in_tx (l.2125), refresh_incoming_links_for_path (l.2264-2350), latest_page_id_for_link; lint.rs dangling cross-project links (l.211-240)
mechanisms.limitations: There are no Pin dependencies (always latest) and no invalidation: re-pointing silently changes what a dependent sees, and dependents are never marked stale or re-validated. Links derived from the body get wiped on rewrite, so programmatic edges are fragile (the code itself says so in lint.rs l.313-318).
mechanisms.why: This is a useful example of Cur-only dependencies and of what goes wrong without Pin plus invalidation. ContextDB should store typed dependency edges separately from content and keep both the pinned revision and the head.

mechanisms.name: page_evidence provenance plus read-time belief confidence
mechanisms.how_it_works: Every page write may carry evidence rows (source_kind in session|observation|feedback|reconsolidation, source_id), inserted with INSERT OR IGNORE on PK (page_id, kind, source_id). A no-op rewrite still records evidence against the current id. belief::confidence computes, at read time, support = 1 - exp(-breadth/3), where breadth counts distinct sessions plus a capped 0.2 credit for non-session rows. That support is multiplied by a recency factor (floor 0.5, tau 30 days) and by 1/(1+unresolved_contradictions), and clamped at 0.95. Confidence only shades ranking. A supersession always wins regardless of confidence.
mechanisms.evidence: migrations V63__page_evidence.sql; ops.rs insert_evidence_in_tx (l.2176); crates/ai-memory-store/src/belief.rs confidence(), BeliefInputs, CONFIDENCE_CAP
mechanisms.readme_vs_code: implemented (the substrate plus an explain surface; the comments say the ranking authority flip is deferred behind an eval)
mechanisms.limitations: Provenance is a flat list of sources, not an AND/OR justification graph. Removing a source does not retract or invalidate the page, and evidence never propagates.
mechanisms.why: The anti-entrenchment design (distinct sources, a cap below 1, recency floor, and 'supersession beats popularity') is a good ranking policy on top of ContextDB's support counting. The justification DAG itself has to come from elsewhere.

mechanisms.name: Contradiction flagging in ai-memory (declared edges, cosine band, LLM) is advisory only
mechanisms.how_it_works: Three paths, all inside run_lint. (1) Declared contradicts edges from frontmatter or LLM-consolidator relations: reader.contradiction_edges joins links with link_type='contradicts' to the latest pages and reports 'reconcile them', or reports a stale declaration when the target no longer resolves. (2) A5 zero-LLM band: a pairwise cosine scan over at most 60 cold pages, flagging pairs with similarity in [0.4, 0.75) (configurable). The message says the newer page wins 'on a timestamp basis'. (3) An optional LLM contradiction pass. Findings go into a single _lint report page, and nothing is persisted as an edge or blocks anything. Explicit memory_feedback kinds stale|wrong also surface in lint and are cleared implicitly by rewriting the page. Unresolved contradictions lower belief confidence.
mechanisms.evidence: crates/ai-memory-consolidate/src/lint.rs run_lint (l.192-370), detected_contradiction_findings, DEFAULT_CONTRADICTION_SIM_LOW/HIGH (l.485-505); crates/ai-memory-store/src/reader.rs contradiction_edges (l.9183); migrations V37__page_feedback.sql
mechanisms.limitations: Lint runs batch or on demand. It is a heuristic with no truth-maintenance semantics and no PENDING state, and it never propagates to dependents. The cosine band is noisy on single-domain corpora (the code admits this).
mechanisms.why: In ContextDB terms this is a semantic-validity signal. It should set a revision to PENDING or disputed rather than FALSE, which matches ContextDB's 'semantic, not structural' distinction. The band heuristic is a cheap candidate generator.

mechanisms.name: Decay, TTL and tombstones (no dependency invalidation)
mechanisms.how_it_works: Staleness is time-based only. pages.expires_at hides expired pages and the retention sweep later hard-deletes them. A decay score (lambda, salience driven by feedback, access_count) soft-deletes pages via soft_delete_for_decay_if_latest (is_latest=0, superseded_at=now, supersedes NULL). hard_delete_decayed_page_chain removes tombstoned chains after N days with no access. Lint flags episodic pages that are unread and older than stale_days_for(lambda).
mechanisms.evidence: ops.rs soft_delete_for_decay_if_latest (l.3774), hard_delete_decayed_page_chain (l.4011), record_page_feedback (l.3702); crates/ai-memory-store/src/decay.rs; lint.rs rule_based_findings, stale_days_for; migrations V03, V36, V37, V49
mechanisms.limitations: Nothing invalidates a page because something it depends on changed. Staleness depends only on age or usage.
mechanisms.why: This is retention policy, not correctness. ContextDB might add TTL as a separate concern but should not mistake it for invalidation.

mechanisms.name: Admission webhook chain (write-time gate, not action-time)
mechanisms.how_it_works: Wiki::write_page runs a configured chain of HTTP webhooks after building the markdown and before the atomic write, for ops WritePage, Consolidate, Delete, DeleteEventLedger, PurgeProject, PurgeSession, PurgeWorkspace and MoveProject. A webhook can return 200 with a mutated page, return 204 to pass, or return 4xx/5xx; with FailurePolicy::Reject that aborts the write. Loop prevention comes from the X-Memory-Skip-Admission-Chain header. Destructive MCP ops also take a git checkpoint before and after (checkpoint_or_mcp).
mechanisms.evidence: crates/ai-memory-wiki/src/admission.rs (module doc, AdmissionOp, AdmissionFailure, is_admission_unavailable); crates/ai-memory-mcp/src/server.rs memory_delete_page admission_ctx plus checkpoint_or_mcp
mechanisms.limitations: It gates writes into memory, not agent actions in the world. There is no certificate and no check that the context an agent read is still valid.
mechanisms.why: The webhook-chain pattern (mutate, pass or reject, with fail-open or fail-closed per hook) is a reasonable extension point for ContextDB's action-time certificate validation hook.

mechanisms.name: mcp-memory-service versioned update with a guarded supersede and compensation
mechanisms.how_it_works: update_memory_versioned first stores a new memory row (content_hash = hash of the new content, inherited metadata), committed separately. Then, in one transaction, it sets the new row's parent_id=old and version=old+1, and runs UPDATE memories SET superseded_by=new WHERE content_hash=old AND superseded_by IS NULL. If rowcount==0 (a concurrent versioned update already superseded it), it raises, rolls back and deletes the orphan new row (compensation). Default retrieval filters superseded_by IS NULL. get_memory_history walks the lineage with a recursive CTE, and a dangling-winner query finds losers whose superseded_by points at a missing row.
mechanisms.evidence: src/mcp_memory_service/storage/mixins/metadata.py update_memory_versioned (~l.611-735), get_memory_history (~l.737-797), dangling superseded_by listing (~l.799-830); storage/mixins/hybrid.py superseded filter (l.72, 257); storage/migrations/011_memory_evolution_p1.sql
mechanisms.limitations: The new row is stored outside the link transaction, so the 'atomicity' is a saga with a best-effort compensating delete. The guard is the superseded_by IS NULL predicate (an implicit CAS on 'still head'), with no client-supplied expected version. mark_superseded_batch and resolve_conflict overwrite superseded_by without that guard. Identity is content_hash, so there is no stable logical id apart from the lineage root.
mechanisms.why: The guard-on-still-head UPDATE (WHERE superseded_by IS NULL, check rowcount) is a minimal head-CAS idiom. The two-phase store-then-link shows why ContextDB should insert the revision and move the head in a single transaction.

mechanisms.name: mcp-memory-service write-time contradiction detection plus manual resolve
mechanisms.how_it_works: On store(), _detect_conflicts takes the 5 nearest live memories by vec_distance_cosine. It flags a candidate when cosine similarity >= 0.95 and the difflib SequenceMatcher text divergence (1 - ratio) >= 0.20, meaning 'same topic, different words'. _record_conflicts adds the tag conflict:unresolved to both memories and inserts symmetric memory_graph edges with relationship_type='contradicts' (metadata holds similarity, divergence and detected_at). memory_conflicts (get_conflicts) lists unresolved pairs where both sides are live and not superseded. memory_resolve (resolve_conflict) sets loser.superseded_by=winner, sets the winner's confidence to 1.0, and strips the conflict tag. Time-decayed confidence is applied at read time in retrieve_with_staleness when MEMORY_DECAY_WINDOW_DAYS > 0.

analysis.overlap_with_contextdb:
Partial overlap on versioning, CAS and contradictions. None on ContextDB's core TMS features.

What already exists:
- **Immutable revisions plus a logical head.** ai-memory: pages with is_latest, a supersedes chain and a partial unique index on the head. mcp-memory-service: parent_id/version/superseded_by.
- **An optional per-key head CAS.** ai-memory: expected_page_id/create_only, checked in the write transaction. mcp-memory-service: an implicit WHERE superseded_by IS NULL guard.
- **Claim-once state CAS** for handoffs and messages.
- **Time-travel as_of windows.**
- **Flat provenance.** ai-memory page_evidence; mcp-memory-service beliefs.derived_from.
- **Contradiction flagging.** ai-memory: declared contradicts edges plus a cosine band plus an LLM pass, all advisory lint. mcp-memory-service: write-time cosine >= 0.95 plus text divergence >= 0.2, tagging both sides conflict:unresolved and adding contradicts edges, resolved manually by superseding the loser.

What is missing:
- **No dependency-driven transitive invalidation.** ai-memory's links silently re-point to the new head (Cur-only, no Pin) and never mark dependents stale. mcp-memory-service beliefs are re-derived only by a periodic batch, and their contradiction input is effectively dead code (get_edges('CONTRADICTED_BY') is undefined).
- **No AND/OR justification graph and no support counting.** Evidence only shades ranking scores.
- **No PENDING or semantic-validity state.** Closest are mcp-memory-service belief 'disputed' and the conflict:unresolved tag.
- **No first-class alternatives.** A concurrent loser is just an older version in a linear chain.
- **No certified reads and no action-time gating.** ai-memory's admission webhooks gate memory writes only.
analysis.could_contextdb_be_built_as_plugin_on_it:
Not as a true plugin. Partly as a sidecar, and only on ai-memory.

**Why ai-memory falls short as a host:**
- Its only extension point is the HTTP admission webhook chain on writes. That can veto or mutate a page write, but it cannot add read certificates, intercept reads, or hook into propagation.
- Dependency edges live in the links table, which is rebuilt from the page body on every write (replace_links_in_tx). The code itself warns that programmatic edges get wiped.
- Supersession re-points dependents to the new head instead of invalidating them.

**What a sidecar could do:** keep its own justification DAG, keyed by ai-memory page ids, with pinned revisions. It would subscribe through admission webhooks (op=WritePage, Consolidate or Delete) to learn about new heads, then run invalidation and gating outside ai-memory. Agent actions would still need a separate validate call.

**mcp-memory-service is worse as a host.** Identity is the content hash, storage is spread across many backends, and supersession is LWW-style.

**Recommendation:** build ContextDB as its own store and copy these proven patterns into it:
- the partial unique index for one head per key
- the content-hash no-op short-circuit
- expected-head CAS returning the expected and current ids on failure
- a single-writer SQLite actor
- claim-once batons
- as_of windows closed on every retirement path
- an evidence table with anti-entrenchment confidence
- cosine plus text-divergence conflict candidates that set PENDING rather than FALSE
- the MCP tool shape (handoff begin/accept, briefing)

Expose an ai-memory-compatible MCP surface so coding-CLI users can switch.

verification.overlap_verdict: Confirmed. Both projects overlap ContextDB only on immutable revisions plus a head, single-key head CAS, claim-once state CAS, transaction-time as_of windows, flat provenance and advisory or heuristic contradiction flagging. Neither implements dependency-driven transitive invalidation, an AND/OR justification graph with support counting, a PENDING or semantic-validity state, first-class alternatives, certified reads, or action-time gating. Five corrections to the evidence: (1) ai-memory page writes take the shared mutation_lock plus a per-path mutex, and the exclusive guard is only for moves, deletes and purges. (2) mcp-memory-service's versioned-update compensation is a soft delete, so the orphan becomes a tombstone rather than being removed. (3) The belief contradiction input is dead because storage has no .graph attribute, not only because get_edges is undefined. (4) sync_events idempotency does not hold for events whose agent_id is NULL. (5) ai-memory belief evidence credit is 0.2 per non-session row, with the total capped at 1.0.
